blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Saliency-guided coding allocates bits to the regions viewers are most likely to attend, but accurate 360-degree saliency prediction is computationally expensive, an obstacle for low-latency immersive streaming applications such as robot teleoperation. We quantify how much saliency-prediction accuracy actually translates into compression gain. Building on a saliency-guided rate-distortion-optimized (RDO) learned codec, modified so that the training-time latent mask is driven by ground-truth saliency, which yields a single, predictor-agnostic codec, we evaluate saliency predictors spanning two orders of magnitude in compute on both the learned codec and H.265/HEVC. The results show that higher saliency-prediction accuracy yields diminishing compression gains: a lightweight predictor fast enough for live use (52 frames per second) captures 65% of the ground-truth oracle's bit-rate saving, a 3.3x heavier one reaches 74%, and a further 38x increase in compute adds no measurable benefit, on either codec. Therefore, lightweight predictors might also be a practical choice for latency-constrained 360-degree streaming.

blocks.en: I Introduction
blocks.zh: 一. 导言

blocks.en:
A growing range of applications must stream 360-degree video under limited bandwidth and latency constraints:
live video surveillance and remote site inspection, virtual attendance of live events, and, most demandingly, immersive teleoperation of robots.
Teleoperation is a particularly demanding application because it simultaneously stresses bandwidth, latency, and compute constraints; hence, we take teleoperation as the primary example.
Teleoperation keeps a human in the loop when robots cannot yet operate autonomously, such as in telesurgery, GPS-denied drone piloting, underwater and planetary exploration, and industrial maintenance. In these settings, the operator’s situational awareness is often the limiting factor.
A conventional 2D camera
feed is frequently insufficient; 360-degree video viewed through a HMD ( HMD ) provides a more natural telepresence interface.
These three constraints are coupled: any pre- or post-processing introduced to save bandwidth itself adds to the end-to-end latency-compute budget.

blocks.en:
Three families of methods address 360-degree streaming: (i) Tiled/viewport streaming [ 1 ] requires head-pose prediction and degrades under fast head motion;
(ii) foveated streaming [ 2 ] requires fast eye tracking and is purely reactive;
and (iii) saliency/content-aware [ 3 ] coding.
Saliency-aware coding is predictive and client(operator)-agnostic, but its cost moves to the saliency prediction model.
Both alternatives (viewport and foveated streaming) also allocate quality by viewing geometry alone, yet human attention is content-dependent [ 4 ] .
Salient details remain perceivable in the periphery even when not gazed
upon, and purely gaze-driven quality reduction produces noticeable peripheral
artifacts [ 5 ] .
We therefore explored saliency-guided coding, which allocates bits by content ( Figure 1 ) and degrades gracefully toward uniform-quality coding when the prediction is poor.
No 360-degree saliency predictor today is simultaneously accurate, real-time, and compression-friendly: the most accurate models rely on heavy computation on full equirectangular frames, and expensive temporal modelling, so predictors
that win on accuracy lose on latency and compute and do not fit a teleoperation workload.
This motivates our research question: how much does saliency-prediction accuracy actually translate into compression gain?

blocks.en:
We conducted a controlled study to examine how accurate a saliency
model must be to meaningfully improve 360-degree image compression.
Our key findings are as follows: • We tested four different saliency sources on a fixed neural codec, ranging
from a lightweight model ( ≈ \approx 305 GFLOPs) to a very heavy one
( ≈ \approx 39,000 GFLOPs), with correlation coefficients (CC) ranging from
0.66 (moderate accuracy) to 1.0 (Oracle/perfect). The results show that a
moderately accurate predictor already achieves about 70 70 – 75 % 75\% of the
bitrate savings that would be possible with a perfect “oracle” (which
uses ground-truth saliency). In contrast, a predictor that is 38 times
more expensive and more accurate adds no measurable additional gain; • The same ordering of predictors holds on a transform/block-based hybrid codec (HEVC saliency-RDO):
there too the heaviest predictor adds nothing.
A synthetic accuracy sweep further shows that current predictors sit below the accuracy at which the learned codec’s gain levels off ( CC ( CC ) ≈ 0.8 {}\approx{}0.8 – 0.9 0.9 ). The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews background and related work, Section III the methodology, Section IV the experimental setup, Section V the results,
and Section VI concludes.

blocks.en: II Background and Related Work
blocks.zh: 二. 背景和有关工作

blocks.en:
This section first defines the two core notions the paper rests on, image
coding and visual saliency, then covers 360-degree streaming and
saliency-aware coding ( Section II-A ), 360-degree saliency
prediction ( Section II-B ), saliency-guided compression in both
codec families ( Section II-C ), and the gap we address
( Section II-D ).
An Image codec compresses a picture into a bit-stream by transforming,
quantizing, and entropy-coding its content, trading rate (the bit-rate, i.e.,
the number of coded bits per pixel) against distortion.
Transform/block-based hybrid codecs, built from hand-designed transforms, such as JPEG and the intra mode of H.265/HEVC, set per-block quality with a QP ( QP ),
whereas learned codecs train an auto-encoder end-to-end under a rate-distortion
objective [ 6 , 7 ] , with variable-rate variants avoiding one model per rate point [ 8 ] .
A Saliency model , in turn, predicts where human attention falls, producing a per-pixel fixation-probability map whose accuracy is scored against eye-tracking ground truth using the CC , NSS ( NSS ), KLD ( KLD ), and AUCJ ( AUCJ ).
Both problems are harder for ODI : the ERP ( ERP ) format
oversamples the poles and viewing is equator-biased, so quality is assessed
with sphere-aware metrics such as WSPSNR ( WSPSNR ) [ 9 ] , and the most
accurate 360-degree saliency predictors are also the most computationally
expensive.

blocks.en: II-A 360-degree Streaming and Saliency-Aware Coding
blocks.zh: II-A 360度的流度和显著度-智能编码

blocks.en:
Of the three streaming families introduced in Section I , we focus on
saliency and content-aware coding because its latency-critical cost is upstream of transmission and tunable through model choice, which suits a teleoperation workload:
tiled/viewport and foveated streaming incur additional latency by tracking the operator’s head or gaze,
whereas saliency-aware (predictive) coding biases the encoder’s bit allocation
toward regions attention is likely to visit before the stream leaves the robot.
Saliency-aware coding has been used inside both block-based hybrid and learned codecs: in HEVC,
Hadizadeh and Bajić [ 10 ] and Chiang et al. [ 3 ] adjust the per-block QP from a saliency map;
in learned codecs, the saliency map modulates the distortion loss and (or) is used as
a latent-space mask [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] .

blocks.en: II-B Saliency Prediction for 360-degree Content
blocks.zh: II-B 360度内容的显著预测

blocks.en:
In recent years, a number of 360-degree saliency predictors have been proposed, with different accuracy and compute footprints.
SalGAN360 [ 14 ] extends a 2D GAN ( GAN )-based predictor to
omnidirectional content by predicting on cube-map faces and fusing the projections.
ATSal [ 15 ] uses a dual-stream design that combines a global attention stream with a local recurrent stream on cube-map patches
(only the “attention” stream of ATSal is used as a predictor in our experiments; see Section III-B ).
The dual-stream detector of Güngördü and Tekalp [ 11 ] essentially extends ATSal by coupling Attention and Expert streams with coordinate-refinement [ 16 ] and fusion sub-networks.
We employ this detector to generate saliency maps for the baseline learned codec adopted in this study.

blocks.en: II-C Saliency-Guided Compression

blocks.en:
Saliency-guided compression has been studied in both codec families.
In learned compression, RDO ( RDO ) beyond the training objective is a topic in
its own right: Schäfer et al. [ 17 ] optimize the
quantized latents of a trained network per image at encoding time, and Brand et al. [ 18 ] obtain a block-partitioning-like dynamic RDO by training a hierarchical autoencoder against a transmitted
latent-space mask. Saliency-guided codecs instead make the objective itself
attention-aware: learned variants typically combine a saliency-weighted
distortion loss with latent-space masking, so the rate term itself becomes
saliency-aware.
Ma et al. [ 12 ] introduced an ROI ( ROI ) variant of end-to-end learned image compression;
Patel et al. [ 13 ] applied saliency-driven perceptual coding to 2D images.
On the block-based hybrid codec side,
Chiang et al. [ 3 ] implement a per- CTU ( CTU ) Δ \Delta QP map for 360-degree HEVC.
Interestingly, Cai et al. [ 19 ] observed qualitatively that in 2D ROI image coding,
“more accurate” region prediction does not monotonically translate into coding gain.
Closest to the present study, for 360-degree content Güngördü and Tekalp [ 11 ] combine ELIC ( ELIC ) with a QVRF ( QVRF ) variable-rate mechanism and a dual-stream saliency predictor,
the configuration we build on ( Section III ).
They compare several 360-degree saliency predictors on prediction accuracy alone and use a single saliency prediction model in compression,
leaving the effect of saliency prediction accuracy on coding gain unexamined.

blocks.en: II-D Research Gap
blocks.zh: 二-D 研究差距

blocks.en:
Although saliency and ROI -guided coding has been applied to
360-degree compression in both the learned and block-based hybrid codec
families, no existing work examines the added cost of saliency prediction in
the 360-degree domain under low-latency constraints.
As just noted for the closest baseline [ 11 ] ,
none relates predictor accuracy or compute to the resulting RDO coding gain.
The open question is therefore quantitative:
how much coding gain does saliency accuracy actually yield for 360-degree compression
across a wide accuracy–complexity range, and is that relationship codec-specific?
We answer it by comparing four saliency sources, and a synthetic accuracy
sweep, on a fixed predictor-agnostic learned codec and on HEVC saliency-RDO.
To our knowledge this is the first study to quantify this relationship for
360-degree content, and the answer is not the expected monotone one: the
most accurate predictor is not the best.

blocks.en: III-A System Overview
blocks.zh: 三-A 系统概览

blocks.en:
The system operates as a linear pipeline: a saliency predictor computes a
per-pixel attention map from the captured ERP frame, a saliency-guided
encoder uses that map to bias its rate allocation, and the bit-stream is
transmitted, decoded, and rendered in the operator’s HMD .
The compression stage itself ( Figure 2 ) couples two networks across a
single interface, the saliency map. A saliency network estimates where
attention falls, and the learned codec consumes the map twice: as a weight on
the distortion term of its training objective and as a multiplicative mask on
part of the latent representation, so that bits are steered toward salient
regions. The map is used only at the encoder and is never transmitted, leaving
the decoder unchanged [ 11 ] . The same map can instead drive a per-block QP offset in a standard
HEVC encoder (the block-based hybrid codec configuration of the study).

blocks.en: III-D Training the Latent Mask with Ground-Truth Saliency

blocks.en:
The baseline and the ROI codecs we build upon [ 11 , 12 ] hold
the saliency (or ROI ) network fixed/essentially-frozen while the compression network is being trained,
and feed its predicted saliency map into the training-time latent masking
( [ 11 , Eq. 1] ). Although the two networks train separately,
the training-time mask couples the codec to the predictor’s error statistics ( [ 11 , Eqs. 1–3] ),
so changing the predictor requires retraining the codec.
We instead replace the Saliency Network ( Figure 2 ) with GT saliency masks during training time ( Eq. 1 ) and
substitute a Saliency predictor network only at inference.
The learned latent masking is then independent of any predictor,
so one GT -trained compression checkpoint serves every saliency source.
This makes the controlled comparison at the heart of this study practical:
every predictor is scored on the same codec, not affected by per-predictor training.

blocks.en: VI Conclusion and Future Work
blocks.zh: 六. 结论和今后的工作

blocks.en:
Increasing saliency-prediction accuracy yields progressively smaller coding gains for 360-degree saliency-guided compression: on the learned codec, a mid-accuracy,
near-real-time predictor captures about three quarters of the oracle’s
bit-rate saving ( 74 % 74\% ), a lightweight real-time predictor (52 FPS) still
captures roughly two thirds ( 65 % 65\% ), while a far heavier, more accurate
predictor adds nothing measurable; the same ordering holds on HEVC. A
synthetic accuracy sweep places the learned codec’s knee near CC ≈ 0.8 {}\approx{}0.8 , above all current predictors, whereas HEVC keeps
gaining up to the oracle.
The practical takeaway for
latency-constrained 360-degree streaming (immersive teleoperation included): a lightweight predictor already delivers most of the attainable coding gain,
so the saliency stage fits comfortably within the latency constraint,
and compute is better invested in the codec itself than in pursuing saliency-metric state of the art.
The 25- ODI test split and the dataset shift relative to the 2017
baseline are the fixed comparison context, identical for every method;
the study is limited to image-only scope.
Future work extends the study to 360-degree video within the latency constraint and
to lightweight saliency proxies built from real-time detectors.
